lecture: Brainstem II: Cranial Nerve Nuclei and Integrative Pathways

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with hypertension has a small hemorrhage that is confined to the floor of the fourth ventricle on the left side, immediately medial to the sulcus limitans, at the level of the caudal pons. He is awake and his limbs are strong. Facial sensation, hearing, and taste are intact on examination. Which of the following deficits is most likely present?

answers.A: Impaired hearing in the left ear
answers.B: Inability to abduct the left eye
answers.C: Loss of pain sensation over the left face
answers.D: Loss of taste over the left tongue
answers.E: Vertigo with nystagmus toward the right

explanations.A: Hearing depends on the cochlear nuclei, which sit far laterally at the pontomedullary junction rather than adjacent to the midline.
explanations.B: The sulcus limitans divides medially placed motor nuclei from laterally placed sensory nuclei, and the somatic motor nucleus lying just medial to it in the caudal pons is the abducens nucleus.
explanations.C: Facial pain and temperature are handled by the spinal trigeminal nucleus, a general sensory column structure located lateral to the sulcus limitans.
explanations.D: Taste is processed in the solitary nucleus, a visceral sensory structure that lies lateral to the sulcus limitans in the medulla.
explanations.E: Vertigo reflects vestibular nuclear injury, and those special sensory nuclei occupy the dorsolateral tegmentum well lateral to the midline.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman notices that her jaw deviates to the left when she opens her mouth and that she cannot crack nuts on the left side. The left masseter and temporalis feel soft when she clenches. MRI shows a small demyelinating plaque in the lateral tegmentum of the mid-pons involving a single motor nucleus. To which functional column does the affected nucleus belong?

explanations.A: The muscles of mastication are first pharyngeal arch derivatives, so their lower motor neurons in the motor trigeminal nucleus belong to the branchial motor column.
explanations.B: General sensory nuclei relay touch, pain, and temperature from the head rather than driving skeletal muscle.
explanations.C: The parasympathetic column contains preganglionic neurons for smooth muscle and glands, none of which move the mandible.
explanations.D: The somatic motor column supplies skeletal muscle that is not pharyngeal arch derived, such as extraocular and tongue muscles.
explanations.E: The visceral sensory column consists of the solitary nucleus and handles taste and baroreception.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has weakness of the right trapezius and sternocleidomastoid after a penetrating neck wound. Sensation over the face and neck is normal, palate elevation is symmetric, and the tongue protrudes in the midline. MRI of the entire brainstem is unremarkable. Where are the cell bodies of the injured lower motor neurons located?

explanations.A: This region contains the trochlear nucleus, whose axons supply the superior oblique muscle.
explanations.B: The accessory nucleus is essentially a displaced portion of the ventral horn in upper cervical segments, and its axons ascend through the foramen magnum before leaving by the jugular foramen.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nucleus occupies this location and supplies tongue musculature, which is normal here.
explanations.D: The nucleus ambiguus lies here and supplies palatal, pharyngeal, and laryngeal muscles.
explanations.E: The oculomotor and Edinger-Westphal nuclei lie at this level and govern eye movement and pupillary constriction.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden weakness of the right arm and leg with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response on the right. His tongue deviates to the right on protrusion, but the tongue shows no atrophy and no fasciculations. Vital signs are shown. Which site of injury best explains the tongue finding?

answers.A: Left corticobulbar fibers in the internal capsule
answers.B: Left hypoglossal nerve in the neck
answers.C: Left hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla
answers.D: Right corticobulbar fibers in the internal capsule
answers.E: Right hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla

explanations.A: Corticobulbar input to the genioglossus is predominantly crossed, so a left-sided upper motor neuron lesion weakens the right genioglossus and pushes the tongue to the right without denervation atrophy.
explanations.B: A peripheral nerve lesion is a lower motor neuron injury and would produce ipsilateral atrophy and fasciculations, which are absent.
explanations.C: A left nuclear lesion would weaken the left genioglossus and deviate the tongue to the left with wasting of that half.
explanations.D: A right-sided capsular lesion would weaken the left limbs and deviate the tongue to the left.
explanations.E: A right nuclear lesion would deviate the tongue to the right but would also produce right hemitongue atrophy and fasciculations.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman develops a severe headache followed by drooping of the right upper lid. The right pupil measures 7 mm and does not react to light, and the right eye rests depressed and abducted. CT angiography demonstrates an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery compressing the right oculomotor nerve. Which extraocular muscle retains normal innervation?

explanations.A: The inferior oblique is one of the five muscles supplied by the oculomotor nucleus and is paralyzed.
explanations.B: The inferior rectus is oculomotor-innervated, and its loss contributes to the abnormal resting position of the globe.
explanations.C: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve, so its unopposed pull abducts the eye in a complete oculomotor palsy.
explanations.D: The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nucleus, and its paralysis produces the ptosis described.
explanations.E: The medial rectus is oculomotor-innervated, and its weakness allows the eye to drift laterally.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has acute onset of a droopy left eyelid, a 6-mm unreactive left pupil, and a left eye that rests down and out. Adduction, elevation, and depression of the left eye are absent, but abduction and intorsion are preserved. MRI shows a small intra-axial infarct in the tegmentum. At which level of the brainstem is the lesion?

explanations.A: The caudal midbrain contains the trochlear nucleus, and a lesion there would impair only depression in adduction.
explanations.B: The caudal pons houses the abducens and facial nuclei, so lesions here impair abduction and facial movement.
explanations.C: The mid-medulla contains the hypoglossal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
explanations.D: The mid-pons contains the motor and main sensory trigeminal nuclei, and injury there affects mastication and facial sensation.
explanations.E: The oculomotor and Edinger-Westphal nuclei sit in the rostral midbrain tegmentum, so a lesion there paralyzes four of the extraocular muscles, the levator, and the pupillary sphincter while sparing the abducens- and trochlear-innervated muscles.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis develops vertical diplopia. MRI shows a discrete plaque in the dorsal tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus, involving a small ovoid nucleus that appears indented into a large adjacent white matter bundle described as an egg sitting in a cup. Which structure forms the cup around this nucleus?

answers.A: Central tegmental tract of the tegmentum

explanations.A: The central tegmental tract runs ventrolaterally in the tegmentum carrying rubro-olivary fibers to the inferior olive.
explanations.B: The lateral lemniscus lies laterally at this level and appears as lobster claws grasping the inferior colliculus.
explanations.C: The medial lemniscus has rotated to a dorsolateral position by the midbrain and does not encase any motor nucleus.
explanations.D: The trochlear nucleus is indented into the dorsal surface of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which yokes the extraocular motor nuclei together.
explanations.E: The spinothalamic tract runs laterally throughout the brainstem alongside the medial lemniscus in the midbrain.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is thrown from a bicycle and strikes the back of his head. He now has vertical double vision that worsens when he looks down and to the right and he compensates by tilting his head toward the right shoulder. MRI shows injury to the left trochlear nerve within the ambient cistern. The injured axons arise from which structure?

explanations.A: The abducens nucleus supplies the ipsilateral lateral rectus and drives horizontal, not vertical, gaze.
explanations.B: The left oculomotor nucleus supplies five extraocular muscles on the left, none of which is the superior oblique.
explanations.C: A left trochlear nuclear lesion would give rise to a right trochlear nerve palsy because the fibers decussate before exiting.
explanations.D: The right oculomotor nucleus supplies right-sided extraocular muscles and the pupil, which are unaffected.
explanations.E: Trochlear fibers cross completely within the dorsal midbrain before exiting, so the axons in the left trochlear nerve originate from the right trochlear nucleus.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy has headaches, impaired upgaze, and difficulty reading and descending stairs, with vertical diplopia in both eyes. MRI reveals a pineal region germinoma compressing the dorsal surface of the midbrain just caudal to the inferior colliculi. Which cranial nerve is most vulnerable to compression at this location?

explanations.A: The abducens nerve leaves ventrally at the pontomedullary junction near the pyramids.
explanations.B: The facial nerve exits ventrolaterally at the cerebellopontine angle.
explanations.C: The oculomotor nerve exits ventrally into the interpeduncular fossa after passing through the red nucleus.
explanations.D: The trigeminal nerve enters and exits laterally through the middle cerebellar peduncle at the mid-pons.
explanations.E: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally, emerging just below the inferior colliculi after coursing around the periaqueductal gray.

questions.question: A 28-year-old obese woman has 6 weeks of headache, transient visual obscurations, and horizontal diplopia. Neither eye abducts past the midline, but adduction, vertical gaze, and pupils are normal, and fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Lumbar puncture results are shown. The nerve responsible for the abduction deficit exits the brainstem at which site?

answers.B: Dorsal midbrain, below the inferior colliculus

explanations.A: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.
explanations.B: This is the dorsal exit point of the trochlear nerve, which would cause vertical rather than horizontal diplopia.
explanations.C: The oculomotor nerve emerges here, and its injury would add ptosis and a dilated pupil.
explanations.D: The abducens nerve courses ventrally from the caudal pons and exits at the pontomedullary junction next to the pyramid, where its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to stretch from raised intracranial pressure.
explanations.E: The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves emerge from the post-olivary sulcus of the medulla.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has 1 week of horizontal diplopia that is worst on left gaze. The left eye sits slightly adducted at rest and does not abduct past the midline. On attempted left gaze the right eye adducts fully, and on right gaze both eyes move normally. Pupils, lids, and facial strength are normal. Which structure is most likely injured?

explanations.A: An isolated lateral rectus palsy with intact adduction of the fellow eye on gaze toward the lesion indicates injury to the abducens nerve after it has left the nucleus, sparing the internuclear signal to the contralateral medial rectus.
explanations.B: A nuclear lesion would also prevent the right eye from adducting during left gaze, producing a complete left conjugate gaze palsy.
explanations.C: A left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes failure of left eye adduction on right gaze, but right gaze is normal here.
explanations.D: A right abducens nerve lesion would prevent abduction of the right eye instead.
explanations.E: A right paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion would abolish conjugate gaze to the right, which is preserved.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man undergoes a right carotid endarterectomy. On the first postoperative day his speech is slurred and his tongue deviates toward the right when protruded. Palate elevation is symmetric, shoulder shrug is symmetric, and strength in all four limbs is normal. Weakness of which muscle best explains the tongue finding?

explanations.A: A weak left genioglossus would allow the intact right muscle to push the tongue toward the left.
explanations.B: The palatoglossus is a palatal muscle supplied by the vagus nerve and elevates the tongue base rather than protruding it.
explanations.C: Each genioglossus protrudes the tongue toward the opposite side, so with the right muscle denervated by hypoglossal injury the unopposed left muscle drives the tongue toward the right.
explanations.D: The hyoglossus depresses the tongue and its isolated weakness does not cause deviation on protrusion.
explanations.E: The right palatoglossus is vagally innervated and its weakness would produce palatal, not lingual, asymmetry.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman has a skull base tumor that completely transects the left hypoglossal nerve within the hypoglossal canal. Examination 3 months later shows marked wasting and fasciculations of the left half of the tongue with deviation to the left on protrusion. Which muscle acting on the tongue retains its normal innervation?

explanations.A: The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve and is paralyzed.
explanations.B: The hyoglossus is hypoglossal-innervated and would be denervated along with the rest of the hemitongue.
explanations.C: The palatoglossus is the sole tongue-associated muscle supplied by the vagus nerve through the nucleus ambiguus, so it escapes a hypoglossal lesion.
explanations.D: The styloglossus is the third extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
explanations.E: Intrinsic tongue muscles, including the vertical fibers, are all hypoglossal-innervated and atrophy after nerve transection.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has 6 months of progressive hoarseness, choking on liquids, and difficulty lifting her right shoulder. Examination shows a paralyzed right vocal cord, absent right palatal elevation, and right trapezius atrophy. Tongue protrusion is midline and tongue bulk is normal. Which skull base opening is most likely involved by her tumor?

explanations.A: The foramen magnum transmits the accessory nerve into the cranial cavity but not the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerves.
explanations.B: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and the lesser petrosal nerve.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal canal transmits only cranial nerve XII, which is spared given the normal midline tongue.
explanations.D: Cranial nerves IX, X, and XI all leave the skull together through the jugular foramen, so a mass there produces combined palatal, laryngeal, and trapezius weakness with a normal tongue.
explanations.E: The stylomastoid foramen transmits the facial nerve and its involvement would cause hemifacial paralysis.

questions.question: A 39-year-old man undergoes excisional biopsy of a lymph node in the right posterior triangle of the neck. Two weeks later the right scapula sits lower and lateral, and he cannot elevate the right arm above shoulder height. Head turning is full and symmetric in both directions, and neck flexion is strong. Which action is most likely weak on examination?

answers.A: Depressing the right shoulder against resistance
answers.B: Elevating the right shoulder against resistance
answers.D: Turning the head to the left against resistance
answers.E: Turning the head to the right against resistance

explanations.A: Shoulder depression is performed largely by the latissimus dorsi and pectoralis minor, which are supplied by other nerves.
explanations.B: The accessory nerve reaches the trapezius after crossing the posterior triangle, so an injury distal to the sternocleidomastoid branches leaves shoulder elevation weak while head turning is spared.
explanations.C: Neck flexion depends on both sternocleidomastoid muscles acting together, and these were innervated proximal to the site of injury.
explanations.D: Turning the head to the left requires the right sternocleidomastoid, whose nerve supply was given off before the posterior triangle.
explanations.E: Turning the head to the right requires the left sternocleidomastoid, which is entirely unaffected.

questions.question: A 59-year-old woman has an infarct involving the hypoglossal nucleus. Her physician is reviewing the functional organization of brainstem nuclei and wants to identify another nucleus that shares the same functional column, because it likewise supplies skeletal muscle that is not derived from a pharyngeal arch. Which nucleus belongs to that same column?

answers.B: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

explanations.A: The abducens nucleus supplies the lateral rectus, an extraocular muscle of somitic rather than pharyngeal arch origin, placing it in the somatic motor column with the hypoglossal nucleus.
explanations.B: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is a parasympathetic column nucleus supplying thoracic and abdominal viscera.
explanations.C: The facial nucleus supplies second pharyngeal arch derivatives and therefore belongs to the branchial motor column.
explanations.D: The nucleus ambiguus supplies third and fourth arch derivatives of the pharynx and larynx and is branchial motor.
explanations.E: The solitary nucleus is the sole visceral sensory nucleus of the brainstem and has no motor output to muscle.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has 3 weeks of dysarthria. Examination shows atrophy and fasciculations of the left half of the tongue with deviation to the left, but normal limb strength, normal palatal elevation, and normal facial movement. At which level would an axial section demonstrate the responsible nucleus?

explanations.A: The caudal midbrain contains the trochlear nucleus and the inferior colliculus.
explanations.B: The caudal pons contains the abducens and facial nuclei together with three of the vestibular nuclei.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nucleus lies in the mid-medulla just beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, with its axons exiting in the pre-olivary sulcus between the pyramid and inferior olive.
explanations.D: The mid-pons contains the motor and main sensory trigeminal nuclei and the trapezoid body.
explanations.E: The rostral midbrain contains the oculomotor and Edinger-Westphal nuclei, the red nucleus, and the substantia nigra.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with multiple prior lacunar strokes has a brisk jaw jerk, a hyperactive gag reflex, emotional lability, and slow spastic speech, with no tongue atrophy. His physician explains that bilateral interruption of descending cortical fibers to brainstem motor nuclei is responsible. Where do these descending fibers cross the midline before reaching their target nucleus?

answers.A: Caudal medulla, at the pyramidal decussation
answers.C: Just rostral to the target cranial nerve nucleus
answers.D: Midbrain, at the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles
answers.E: Spinal cord, in the anterior white commissure

explanations.A: The pyramidal decussation is where corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract for limb muscles.
explanations.B: The posterior limb of the internal capsule is a site where these fibers descend but not where they cross.
explanations.C: Corticobulbar fibers travel along the medial edge of the corticospinal tract and peel off to decussate just above the level of the cranial nerve nucleus they innervate, and because most such nuclei also retain some ipsilateral input, bilateral lesions are required for a pseudobulbar picture.
explanations.D: The superior cerebellar peduncles decussate in the midbrain carrying cerebellar output toward the red nucleus and thalamus.
explanations.E: The anterior white commissure is where second-order spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with a Pancoast tumor has a mild droop of the right upper lid. Extraocular movements are full and the lid elevates fully on voluntary effort, though it fatigues at rest. The right side of his face does not sweat. Pupil measurements are shown. Weakness of which muscle best explains the eyelid finding?

explanations.A: The dilator pupillae is also sympathetically denervated and explains the anisocoria that worsens in dim light, but it has no action on the eyelid.
explanations.B: Loss of this oculomotor-innervated muscle produces a complete ptosis accompanied by extraocular weakness and a dilated pupil.
explanations.C: The orbicularis oculi closes the eye and is supplied by the facial nerve, so its weakness would cause lagophthalmos instead.
explanations.D: The superior rectus elevates the globe rather than the lid, and elevation is full in this patient.
explanations.E: The superior tarsal muscle is smooth muscle driven by postganglionic sympathetic fibers, so interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway produces the partial ptosis of Horner syndrome with miosis and anhidrosis.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man is evaluated for vertical diplopia after a fall. MRI demonstrates a small cavernous malformation in the dorsal tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus, adjacent to the periaqueductal gray. Which somatic motor nucleus would be identified in an axial histologic section taken at this level?

explanations.A: The abducens nucleus lies one level lower, in the dorsal caudal pons beneath the facial colliculus.
explanations.B: The accessory nucleus is not in the brainstem at all but in the ventral horn of upper cervical cord segments.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nucleus lies in the mid-medulla beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle.
explanations.D: The oculomotor nucleus lies one level higher, at the rostral midbrain adjacent to the superior colliculus.
explanations.E: The trochlear nucleus occupies the dorsal tegmentum of the caudal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus, embedded in the medial longitudinal fasciculus just ventral to the periaqueductal gray.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man has a nasopharyngeal carcinoma that has destroyed the right vagus nerve just below the jugular foramen. He is hoarse, chokes on liquids, and on phonation the right side of the soft palate fails to rise. Facial sensation and jaw strength are normal. Which palatal muscle retains its normal innervation?

explanations.A: The levator veli palatini is supplied by the nucleus ambiguus through the vagus and is the principal muscle whose paralysis causes the palatal droop.
explanations.B: The musculus uvulae is vagally innervated and its loss contributes to deviation of the uvula toward the intact side.
explanations.C: The palatoglossus is the one tongue-associated muscle supplied by the vagus and is therefore also paralyzed.
explanations.D: The palatopharyngeus is a vagally innervated palatal and pharyngeal muscle.
explanations.E: The tensor veli palatini is the sole palatal muscle supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve from the motor trigeminal nucleus, so it escapes a vagal lesion.

questions.question: A 57-year-old woman has a slowly growing mass at the lateral aspect of the mid-pons. She has numbness over the right cheek and weakness of the right muscles of mastication, with the jaw deviating to the right on opening. Hearing and facial movement are normal. The motor axons involved leave the brainstem by passing directly through which structure?

explanations.A: The cerebral peduncle carries descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers through the ventral midbrain.
explanations.B: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries olivocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar fibers into the cerebellum from the medulla.
explanations.C: The motor and sensory roots of the trigeminal nerve traverse the middle cerebellar peduncle to reach the lateral surface of the mid-pons.
explanations.D: The superior cerebellar peduncle conveys cerebellar output, such as the dentatorubral tract, toward the midbrain.
explanations.E: The trapezoid body is a mid-pontine bundle of decussating auditory fibers from the cochlear nuclei.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man requires resection of a floor-of-mouth tumor, and the surgeon warns him that the nerve supplying the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of the digastric may be sacrificed. These two muscles develop from the first pharyngeal arch. The lower motor neurons that supply them are located in which nucleus?

explanations.A: The facial nucleus supplies second arch derivatives, which include the posterior rather than the anterior belly of the digastric.
explanations.B: The hypoglossal nucleus supplies intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, which are somite-derived.
explanations.C: First pharyngeal arch muscles, including the muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior digastric, are supplied by the motor trigeminal nucleus in the mid-pons.
explanations.D: The nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles derived from more caudal arches.
explanations.E: The superior salivatory nucleus is parasympathetic and supplies glands rather than skeletal muscle.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman awakens with complete paralysis of the left side of her face, including the forehead. She reports that ordinary sounds are uncomfortably loud in the left ear, and taste is reduced over the left anterior tongue. Hearing thresholds by audiometry are normal bilaterally and the tympanic membranes appear normal. Paralysis of which muscle best explains her sound intolerance?

explanations.A: The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid and its paralysis causes incomplete eye closure rather than hyperacusis.
explanations.B: The posterior digastric elevates the hyoid during swallowing and has no auditory role.
explanations.C: The stapedius, supplied by the facial nucleus, dampens ossicular movement by stabilizing the stapes, so its paralysis leaves ordinary sounds abnormally loud.
explanations.D: The stylohyoid is a facial nerve target that assists hyoid elevation and does not modulate sound transmission.
explanations.E: The tensor tympani also dampens sound but is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which is intact here given normal facial sensation and mastication.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man has an isolated injury to the right glossopharyngeal nerve after a styloid process fracture. He notes reduced sensation of the right oropharynx and altered taste at the back of the tongue. Palatal elevation is symmetric and his voice is normal. Weakness of which muscle is attributable to the branchial motor component of the injured nerve?

explanations.A: The cricothyroid is a laryngeal muscle supplied by the vagus through the external laryngeal nerve.
explanations.B: The palatopharyngeus receives vagal branchial motor fibers from the nucleus ambiguus.
explanations.C: The salpingopharyngeus is likewise a vagally innervated pharyngeal muscle.
explanations.D: The stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, although its lower motor neurons still reside in the nucleus ambiguus.
explanations.E: The superior constrictor is supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus, explaining the preserved palatal and pharyngeal function.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man has an infarct of the right rostral medulla. He is hoarse and dysphagic, and telemetry shows a resting heart rate that no longer slows appropriately with carotid sinus massage or with a Valsalva maneuver. Findings are shown. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that would normally slow the heart arise from which nucleus?

answers.A: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

explanations.A: The dorsal motor nucleus supplies smooth muscle and glands of the thorax and abdomen rather than cardiac muscle.
explanations.B: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle through the ciliary ganglion.
explanations.C: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies the parotid gland through the otic ganglion.
explanations.D: In addition to its branchial motor neurons for the palate, pharynx, and larynx, the nucleus ambiguus provides the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that travel in the vagus to cardiac terminal ganglia, which is why hoarseness accompanies the loss of vagal cardiac tone.
explanations.E: The solitary nucleus is the visceral sensory terminus for baroreceptor input and forms the afferent rather than efferent limb.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman has a dilated right pupil that constricts poorly and slowly to light but does react to a near target. Accommodation is sluggish and the deep tendon reflexes are absent. Extraocular movements are full and there is no ptosis, and the physician concludes that the ciliary ganglion is damaged. Postganglionic axons from that ganglion reach the sphincter pupillae by traveling in which nerve?

explanations.A: The auriculotemporal nerve of V3 carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
explanations.B: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic facial parasympathetics toward the pterygopalatine ganglion.
explanations.C: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic glossopharyngeal fibers to the otic ganglion.
explanations.D: The nasociliary nerve is the sensory branch of V1 that supplies the cornea and forms the afferent limb of the blink reflex.
explanations.E: Postganglionic neurons of the ciliary ganglion send axons in the short ciliary nerves, branches associated with the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, to reach the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man has a thunderclap headache followed by drooping of the right lid and double vision. The right pupil measures 6 mm and is unreactive to direct or consensual light, and the right eye is deviated down and out. The parasympathetic axons whose compression accounts for the pupillary finding originate from cell bodies in which structure?

explanations.A: Preganglionic parasympathetic neurons in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus send axons that travel superficially in the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, making them especially vulnerable to extrinsic compression by an aneurysm.
explanations.B: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies the parotid gland by way of the glossopharyngeal nerve.
explanations.C: The oculomotor nucleus contains somatic lower motor neurons for the extraocular muscles and levator, explaining the ophthalmoplegia and ptosis but not the fixed pupil.
explanations.D: The pretectal nucleus is an interneuronal relay in the pupillary light reflex and does not send axons into the oculomotor nerve.
explanations.E: The superior salivatory nucleus supplies lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands through the facial nerve.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man has a skull base fracture that transects the nerve of the pterygoid canal on the left. He has a dry left nasal cavity and reduced left tear production, and the left nasal mucosa is persistently pale and non-congested. The deep petrosal component of the injured nerve carries which type of fibers?

answers.A: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion
answers.B: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the internal carotid plexus
answers.C: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve
answers.D: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the upper thoracic cord
answers.E: Special sensory taste fibers from the palatal mucosa

explanations.A: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers leave the pterygopalatine ganglion on branches of V2 after the synapse and are not part of the deep petrosal nerve.
explanations.B: The deep petrosal nerve arises from the carotid plexus surrounding the internal carotid artery and carries postganglionic sympathetic fibers that pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing to reach the oronasal mucosa.
explanations.C: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers are carried by the greater petrosal nerve, the other contributor to the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
explanations.D: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers synapse in the superior cervical ganglion before any fibers join the carotid plexus.
explanations.E: Taste fibers from the palate travel with the greater petrosal nerve back toward the geniculate ganglion and solitary nucleus.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman undergoes middle ear surgery, during which a small nerve crossing the tympanic membrane is divided. Afterward she reports a metallic taste and loss of taste over the left anterior tongue, and salivary output from the left submandibular duct is reduced. Tearing and parotid flow are normal. The interrupted preganglionic fibers were destined to synapse in which ganglion?

explanations.A: The ciliary ganglion relays Edinger-Westphal fibers to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
explanations.B: The geniculate ganglion houses sensory cell bodies of the facial nerve and contains no parasympathetic synapse.
explanations.C: The otic ganglion relays glossopharyngeal fibers to the parotid gland, whose secretion is preserved.
explanations.D: The pterygopalatine ganglion relays greater petrosal fibers to the lacrimal gland and oronasal mucosa, and tearing is normal here.
explanations.E: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus that synapse in the submandibular ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman has decreased tear production in the right eye after resection of a pterygopalatine fossa tumor. Corneal sensation is intact, facial movement is normal, and taste is preserved. Her physician explains that the postganglionic neurons supplying the lacrimal gland lie in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Their axons reach the gland by traveling along which nerves?

answers.C: Deep petrosal and carotid plexus nerves

explanations.A: These carry postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
explanations.B: These carry postganglionic fibers from the submandibular ganglion to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
explanations.C: These carry sympathetic rather than parasympathetic fibers toward the pterygopalatine ganglion.
explanations.D: These are the routes taken by ciliary ganglion fibers reaching intraocular smooth muscle.
explanations.E: Postganglionic fibers join the zygomatic nerve of V2, which sends a communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve of V1 within the lateral orbit, illustrating the rule that postganglionic parasympathetics of the head ride on branches of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man had a right superficial parotidectomy 9 months ago. He now notices that the skin overlying the right parotid bed flushes and sweats profusely whenever he eats, though it does not sweat with exercise. Regenerating parasympathetic axons have been misdirected to sweat glands. Before the surgery, these preganglionic axons synapsed in which ganglion?

explanations.A: The ciliary ganglion serves intraocular smooth muscle by way of the short ciliary nerves.
explanations.B: Preganglionic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve and its lesser petrosal branch to synapse in the otic ganglion, whose postganglionic axons then reach the parotid on the auriculotemporal nerve.
explanations.C: The pterygopalatine ganglion serves the lacrimal gland and oronasal mucosa.
explanations.D: The submandibular ganglion serves the submandibular and sublingual glands through the lingual nerve.
explanations.E: The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic and supplies the facial sweat glands that are normally recruited by heat and exercise.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man undergoes bilateral truncal vagotomy for intractable peptic ulcer disease. He subsequently has delayed gastric emptying and reduced intestinal motility. His surgeon explains that parasympathetic innervation supplied by the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus extends only to a defined point along the gut. Which structure is the most distal target of these fibers?

answers.B: Proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
answers.E: Splenic flexure and distal transverse colon

explanations.A: The descending colon receives parasympathetic supply from the pelvic splanchnic nerves of S2 through S4.
explanations.B: Preganglionic fibers from the dorsal motor nucleus supply smooth muscle and glands of the thorax and abdomen as far as roughly two-thirds of the way across the transverse colon, synapsing in terminal ganglia within the organ wall.
explanations.C: The rectum is supplied by pelvic splanchnic parasympathetics, not the vagus.
explanations.D: The sigmoid colon lies well beyond the vagal territory and is served by sacral parasympathetics.
explanations.E: The distal transverse colon and splenic flexure mark the beginning of the pelvic splanchnic territory rather than the end of the vagal one.

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman with a brainstem glioma reports a gritty right eye, dry mouth when she eats, and thick saliva. Testing shows reduced right-sided tear production and reduced submandibular and sublingual salivary flow, while parotid flow is normal. Facial strength is intact. Results are shown. Which nucleus is most likely involved?

answers.A: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

explanations.A: The dorsal motor nucleus governs thoracic and abdominal viscera and has no role in tearing or salivation.
explanations.B: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus governs pupillary constriction and accommodation.
explanations.C: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies only the parotid gland, whose secretion is preserved here.
explanations.D: The nucleus ambiguus is branchial motor to the pharynx and larynx and supplies cardiac parasympathetics.
explanations.E: The superior salivatory nucleus sends preganglionic fibers in the facial nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion for the lacrimal gland and oronasal mucosa and to the submandibular ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands, exactly the combination affected here.

questions.question: A newborn with hemifacial microsomia has hypoplasia of structures derived from the second pharyngeal arch, and imaging shows an abnormally small motor nucleus in the caudal pons on the affected side. Which nucleus contains the lower motor neurons for the skeletal muscles derived from that arch?

explanations.A: The abducens nucleus is somatic motor to the lateral rectus, a muscle of somitic origin.
explanations.B: The facial nucleus supplies second arch derivatives, including the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of the digastric.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles derived from occipital somites.
explanations.D: The motor trigeminal nucleus supplies first arch derivatives such as the muscles of mastication.
explanations.E: The nucleus ambiguus supplies muscles derived from the third and more caudal arches.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has a trigeminal schwannoma at Meckel cave on the left. She has numbness over the left face, wasting of the left temporalis, and complains that everyday sounds are uncomfortably loud in the left ear. Facial movement, taste, and audiometric thresholds are normal. Paralysis of which muscle best explains the sound intolerance?

explanations.A: The levator veli palatini elevates the palate and is supplied by the vagus through the nucleus ambiguus.
explanations.B: The medial pterygoid is a muscle of mastication whose weakness affects chewing but not sound transmission.
explanations.C: The mylohyoid elevates the floor of the mouth and has no auditory function.
explanations.D: The stapedius also dampens sound but is a facial nerve target, and facial movement and taste are intact in this patient.
explanations.E: The tensor tympani is a first arch derivative supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and it dampens loud sound by tensing the tympanic membrane.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is found to have an isolated infarct of the right nucleus ambiguus, with sparing of surrounding tracts and of the solitary and spinal trigeminal nuclei. He is alert with normal limb strength and normal facial sensation. Which finding is most likely on examination?

answers.A: Absent gag sensation when the right oropharynx is touched
answers.B: Deviation of the tongue to the right on protrusion
answers.C: Hoarse voice with the uvula deviating to the left
answers.D: Loss of taste over the right posterior third of the tongue
answers.E: Weakness of the right sternocleidomastoid and trapezius

explanations.A: Gag sensation is the afferent limb carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve to the spinal trigeminal and solitary nuclei, which are spared.
explanations.B: Tongue protrusion depends on the hypoglossal nucleus, which lies medially and is not involved.
explanations.C: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the laryngeal muscles and the levator veli palatini, so its loss produces a paralyzed right vocal cord and a palate that elevates only on the left, drawing the uvula toward the intact side.
explanations.D: Taste from the posterior tongue projects to the solitary nucleus, which is explicitly spared.
explanations.E: These muscles are supplied by the accessory nucleus in the upper cervical cord.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man has an infarct that abolishes reflex salivation from the right parotid gland while leaving tearing, submandibular flow, taste, and all facial movement intact. His physician wants to identify the axial level at which the responsible parasympathetic nucleus would be found. Which level is correct?

explanations.A: The caudal pons contains the superior salivatory nucleus, which serves the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands.
explanations.B: The pyramidal decussation is in the caudal-most medulla and contains no parasympathetic cranial nerve nucleus.
explanations.C: The mid-pons contains the motor and main sensory trigeminal nuclei.
explanations.D: The inferior salivatory nucleus lies in the rostral medulla and sends preganglionic fibers in the glossopharyngeal nerve to the otic ganglion for the parotid gland.
explanations.E: The rostral midbrain houses the Edinger-Westphal nucleus for pupillary constriction and accommodation.

questions.question: A 37-year-old man has complete paralysis of the right side of the face including the forehead. Test results are shown. His physician concludes that the lesion lies along the intratemporal course of the facial nerve. At which point along the nerve is the lesion most likely located?

answers.E: Within the facial nucleus of the pons

explanations.A: A lesion at the cerebellopontine angle is proximal to the greater petrosal branch and would reduce tearing, yet the Schirmer test is symmetric.
explanations.B: A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen is distal to both the stapedial and chorda tympani branches, so hyperacusis and taste loss would not occur.
explanations.C: A lesion distal to the chorda tympani would spare taste, which is absent on the right.
explanations.D: Normal tearing places the lesion beyond the greater petrosal nerve, while an absent stapedial reflex and lost anterior tongue taste place it proximal to the branches to the stapedius and the chorda tympani.
explanations.E: A nuclear lesion would spare taste and lacrimation, which depend on the solitary and superior salivatory nuclei rather than the facial nucleus.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman has reduced salivary output from the left parotid gland after a deep lobe tumor was resected from the infratemporal fossa. Tearing, submandibular flow, taste, and facial movement are all normal. The postganglionic parasympathetic axons that were interrupted travel to the gland along which nerve?

explanations.A: Postganglionic neurons in the otic ganglion send their axons along the auriculotemporal branch of V3 to reach the parotid gland.
explanations.B: The buccal nerve of V3 is a general sensory nerve to the cheek mucosa and skin.
explanations.C: The chorda tympani carries taste and preganglionic fibers destined for the submandibular ganglion.
explanations.D: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic rather than postganglionic fibers and ends by synapsing in the otic ganglion.
explanations.E: The lingual nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the submandibular ganglion to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has a new plaque in the lateral tegmentum of the mid-pons. She cannot feel a cotton wisp, a vibrating tuning fork, or firm pressure over the right side of her face, yet pinprick and cold sensation over the same area are entirely normal. Jaw strength and the jaw jerk are normal. Which structure is most likely involved?

answers.A: Main sensory nucleus of the trigeminal

explanations.A: The main sensory nucleus in the mid-pons handles light touch, pressure, vibration, and conscious proprioception from the head and functions as the cranial analogue of the dorsal column nuclei, so its isolated loss spares pain and temperature.
explanations.B: The mesencephalic nucleus carries muscle stretch information from the muscles of mastication and its loss would blunt the jaw jerk.
explanations.C: The motor trigeminal nucleus supplies the muscles of mastication and would produce jaw weakness rather than sensory loss.
explanations.D: The spinal trigeminal nucleus mediates pain and temperature, which are preserved in this patient.
explanations.E: A ganglion lesion is peripheral and would abolish all sensory modalities together in the affected divisions.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man has a small infarct that damages a compact sensory bundle in the tegmentum of the right rostral pons. He has loss of touch, vibration, pain, and temperature over the left side of the face, with normal facial strength and normal corneal sensation on the right. The second-order axons in this bundle crossed the midline at which site?

answers.A: Anterior white commissure of the spinal cord
answers.B: Caudal medulla, as internal arcuate fibers
answers.C: Dorsal midbrain, above the trochlear nuclei
answers.D: Pons, near the nuclei of origin
answers.E: Rostral medulla, in the trapezoid body

explanations.A: The anterior white commissure is where second-order spinothalamic fibers from the body cross within the spinal cord.
explanations.B: Internal arcuate fibers are the decussating second-order axons of the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus, which serve the body rather than the head.
explanations.C: The dorsal midbrain above the trochlear nuclei is where trochlear motor fibers, not sensory fibers, decussate.
explanations.D: Second-order axons from the main sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei cross the midline in the pons to form the trigeminal lemniscus, so a unilateral pontine lesion of that bundle produces contralateral facial sensory loss.
explanations.E: The trapezoid body carries decussating auditory fibers from the cochlear nuclei toward the superior olivary complex.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden numbness of the entire left half of his body including the left face, with all sensory modalities equally impaired. Strength, coordination, and visual fields are normal, and there are no cranial nerve motor deficits. MRI shows a small lacunar infarct in the thalamus. Which thalamic nucleus contains the affected third-order neurons for the face?

explanations.A: The anterior nucleus is part of the limbic circuit and relays mammillothalamic input to the cingulate gyrus.
explanations.B: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the thalamic relay for the visual pathway.
explanations.C: The medial geniculate nucleus relays auditory information from the inferior colliculus to the temporal lobe.
explanations.D: The ventral posterolateral nucleus receives the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract from the body, not the head.
explanations.E: The trigeminal lemniscus terminates in the ventral posteromedial nucleus, whose third-order neurons project to the face region of the postcentral gyrus.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man has an infarct of the dorsolateral medulla. He has lost pinprick and temperature sensation over the right side of his face and over the left arm and leg, while light touch on the face is preserved. Before synapsing, the first-order facial pain fibers responsible for this deficit descend from the pons within which structure?

explanations.A: The central tegmental tract carries rubro-olivary fibers from the red nucleus to the inferior olive.
explanations.B: The lateral lemniscus is the ascending auditory bundle to the inferior colliculus.
explanations.C: The medial lemniscus carries already-decussated second-order fibers for touch and vibration from the body.
explanations.D: First-order pain and temperature axons entering with cranial nerves V, VII, IX, and X descend in the spinal trigeminal tract, the cranial analogue of Lissauer tract, as far as the upper cervical cord before synapsing in the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
explanations.E: The trigeminal lemniscus contains second-order axons that have already crossed en route to the thalamus.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man with a brainstem cavernoma has lost pinprick sensation over his lips, the mucosa of the anterior oral cavity, and his upper and lower incisors, while pinprick sensation over his forehead, cheeks, and the skin in front of the ears remains normal. Light touch over the whole face is intact. Which portion of the spinal trigeminal nucleus is most likely involved?

answers.A: Main sensory portion in the mid-pons
answers.C: Pars caudalis near the cervical cord
answers.E: Pars oralis in the rostral medulla

explanations.A: The main sensory nucleus mediates light touch and pressure, which are preserved here.
explanations.B: The mesencephalic nucleus carries proprioception from the muscles of mastication and has no cutaneous representation.
explanations.C: The pars caudalis represents the most peripheral onion-skin zones such as the forehead and preauricular region, which are spared.
explanations.D: The pars interpolaris represents the intermediate midface and mentum bands rather than the perioral region.
explanations.E: The somatotopy of the spinal trigeminal nucleus is arranged in concentric onion-skin bands, and the rostral-most pars oralis represents the perioral region, oral cavity, and teeth.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has an infarct restricted to the right spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract in the medulla. In addition to loss of pain sensation over the right face, she is also found to have reduced pain sensation in the right external auditory canal, over the right mastoid skin, and in the right oropharynx. Which explanation best accounts for this broader distribution?

answers.A: Cervical plexus fibers ascend into the nucleus from C2 through C4
answers.B: General sensory fibers of cranial nerves VII, IX, and X also terminate here
answers.C: The nucleus receives bilateral input from both trigeminal ganglia
answers.D: The nucleus receives proprioceptive input from the mesencephalic nucleus
answers.E: The nucleus relays taste fibers from the solitary tract

explanations.A: Cervical plexus fibers supply the skin of the neck and angle of the mandible through their own dorsal root ganglia and dorsal horn, not the trigeminal nucleus.
explanations.B: Despite its name, the spinal trigeminal nucleus receives general sensory input from cranial nerves V, VII, IX, and X, which is why lesions also impair sensation in the ear canal, mastoid skin, and oropharynx.
explanations.C: Trigeminal input to this nucleus is essentially ipsilateral, which is why the deficit is one-sided.
explanations.D: Mesencephalic fibers convey muscle stretch information to the motor trigeminal and main sensory nuclei, not cutaneous sensation.
explanations.E: Taste fibers terminate in the solitary nucleus, a separate visceral sensory structure.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is examined with a finger placed on his chin and tapped with a reflex hammer, which stretches the masseters and produces a brisk closure of the jaw. The afferent limb of this reflex consists of first-order neurons whose cell bodies lie within the brainstem itself. Which structure carries the efferent limb of this reflex?

answers.A: Facial nerve to the orbicularis oris
answers.D: Trigeminal motor root to the masseter
answers.E: Vagus nerve to the levator veli palatini

explanations.A: The facial nerve supplies muscles of facial expression and forms the efferent limb of the corneal blink reflex.
explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies only the stylopharyngeus and serves mainly as an afferent limb for the gag reflex.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles and takes no part in the jaw jerk.
explanations.D: First-order neurons in the mesencephalic nucleus project directly onto lower motor neurons of the motor trigeminal nucleus, whose axons travel in the motor root of V to close the jaw, making this a monosynaptic stretch reflex.
explanations.E: The vagus nerve is the efferent limb of the gag reflex through the nucleus ambiguus.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman has sudden ptosis of the right eyelid and horizontal and vertical diplopia. Visual acuity and visual fields are full in both eyes, and she reports no visual dimming. Results of swinging-flashlight testing are shown. Which structure is most likely damaged?

explanations.A: A left optic nerve lesion would abolish both direct and consensual responses only when the left eye is illuminated.
explanations.B: A unilateral pretectal lesion does not abolish constriction in one pupil to both stimuli, since pretectal projections reach both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
explanations.C: An efferent lesion paralyzes the right sphincter pupillae, so the right pupil fails to constrict regardless of which eye is lit, while the intact left efferent limb keeps the left pupil reactive to both stimuli, and the accompanying ptosis and diplopia confirm oculomotor involvement.
explanations.D: A right optic nerve lesion would abolish both pupillary responses only when the right eye is illuminated and would cause subjective dimming.
explanations.E: A right pretectal lesion would not produce a fixed pupil on one side alone with preserved responses on the other.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man has drooping of the right side of his mouth and cannot wrinkle the right forehead. Facial sensation is normal to pinprick and light touch bilaterally, and he clearly feels the cotton wisp on both corneas. Results of corneal stimulation are shown. Which structure is most likely injured?

explanations.A: A left facial nerve lesion would abolish the left blink to both stimuli, but the left eye blinks normally.
explanations.B: A left trigeminal lesion would abolish both blinks only when the left cornea is stimulated and would produce numbness on the left.
explanations.C: The efferent limb is the facial nerve to the orbicularis oculi, so a right-sided lesion abolishes the right blink whichever cornea is touched while corneal sensation and the fellow eye blink remain normal.
explanations.D: A right trigeminal lesion would abolish both blinks when the right cornea is touched and would render the right cornea insensate.
explanations.E: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance and takes no part in this reflex.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman is examined after a facial injury. Touching the cornea of her intact left eye produces prompt closure of both eyelids simultaneously, and touching the right cornea does the same. Her physician explains that all brainstem reflexes of this type are bilateral. Which anatomic feature best accounts for the bilateral blink after unilateral corneal stimulation?

answers.A: Interneurons from the spinal trigeminal nucleus project to both facial nuclei
answers.B: The corneal afferents decussate within the trigeminal ganglion
answers.C: The facial nerves are joined by a commissure at the geniculate ganglion
answers.D: The main sensory nucleus projects directly to the contralateral cornea
answers.E: The nasociliary nerve supplies both corneas through the orbital septum

explanations.A: Corneal afferents in the nasociliary branch of V1 terminate in the spinal trigeminal nucleus, whose interneurons then project bilaterally onto the facial motor nuclei, generating a direct and a consensual blink.
explanations.B: The trigeminal ganglion contains first-order cell bodies and no decussating fibers.
explanations.C: There is no commissure linking the two facial nerves peripherally, and the crossing occurs centrally within the brainstem.
explanations.D: The main sensory nucleus relays touch and pressure to the thalamus and is not the reflex arc for blinking.
explanations.E: Each nasociliary nerve supplies only the cornea of its own side.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man is evaluated for choking episodes. His voice is normal, both sides of the soft palate elevate briskly and symmetrically on phonation, and the uvula stays midline. Results of oropharyngeal stimulation with a tongue blade are shown. Which structure is most likely injured?

explanations.A: A left-sided afferent lesion would abolish the response when the left oropharynx is stimulated, which is not the case.
explanations.B: A left vagal lesion would leave only the right palate elevating no matter which side is stimulated.
explanations.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so a right-sided lesion renders the right oropharynx functionally numb and no palate elevation occurs on that stimulus, while stimulation of the intact side gives a full bilateral response.
explanations.D: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles and plays no role in the gag reflex.
explanations.E: A right vagal lesion would produce asymmetric palatal elevation with the uvula pulled left regardless of which side is stimulated.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman with a medullary tumor has an absent gag reflex on stimulation of either side of the oropharynx. Palatal elevation on phonation is symmetric and her voice is normal, and taste over the posterior tongue is preserved. The touch afferents from the oropharynx that initiate this reflex terminate in which nucleus?

answers.A: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
answers.B: Main sensory nucleus of the trigeminal

explanations.A: This is a parasympathetic efferent nucleus supplying thoracic and abdominal viscera.
explanations.B: The main sensory nucleus receives light touch and pressure from the face and is not the terminus for oropharyngeal reflex afferents.
explanations.C: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the efferent limb through the vagus, and its intact function is shown by the symmetric palatal elevation on phonation.
explanations.D: The solitary nucleus receives the taste component of glossopharyngeal input, which is preserved here.
explanations.E: General sensory fibers of the glossopharyngeal nerve from the oropharynx project to the spinal trigeminal nucleus, whose interneurons then drive both nuclei ambigui to produce the bilateral gag.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman has episodes of lancinating, electric-shock pain lasting seconds that are triggered by shaving her upper lip or brushing her upper teeth. The pain covers the skin of the cheek, the side of the nose, and the upper gums, but spares the forehead and the mandible. MRI shows a vessel looping onto the trigeminal root. Which division is affected?

answers.C: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
answers.D: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
answers.E: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: The great auricular nerve is a cervical plexus branch supplying the skin over the angle of the mandible and lower ear.
explanations.B: The lesser occipital nerve is also a cervical plexus branch supplying scalp behind the ear.
explanations.C: The mandibular division supplies the skin over the mandible, the lower teeth, and the anterior tongue.
explanations.D: The maxillary division supplies the skin of the midface and side of the nose, most of the nasal cavity, and the maxillary teeth and gums, matching this distribution exactly.
explanations.E: The ophthalmic division supplies the forehead, scalp, and cornea, which are spared.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man receives a complete anesthetic block of the left mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve before dental surgery. He can no longer feel the skin over the body of the mandible, the lower teeth, or the anterior tongue. He is surprised that the skin over the angle of the mandible remains fully sensate. Which nerve supplies that residual area?

answers.B: Buccal branch of the facial nerve

explanations.A: The auriculotemporal nerve is a V3 branch and would be anesthetized by the block.
explanations.B: The buccal branch of the facial nerve is motor to the muscles of facial expression and carries no cutaneous sensation.
explanations.C: Skin over the angle of the mandible and much of the upper neck is supplied by cervical plexus branches arising from the C2 through C4 ventral rami, which lie entirely outside the trigeminal territory.
explanations.D: The inferior alveolar nerve is a V3 branch supplying the lower teeth.
explanations.E: The mental nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the inferior alveolar nerve supplying the chin and lower lip.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man begins coughing forcefully whenever the physician irrigates cerumen from his left external auditory canal. He has no cough with throat examination and no history of lung disease, and his chest radiograph is normal. Sensory fibers from the wall of the external auditory canal that trigger this response travel in which nerve?

answers.C: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: The facial nerve has only a small cutaneous territory over the mastoid region and a bit of the concha.
explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the middle ear cavity and part of the external ear, but the cough response is a vagal reflex.
explanations.C: The maxillary division supplies the midface and nasal cavity, not the ear canal.
explanations.D: The vagus nerve supplies the posterior pinna, external auditory canal, and tympanic membrane, and stimulating this territory can trigger a reflex cough through its central connections in the spinal trigeminal and solitary nuclei.
explanations.E: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance and has no cutaneous distribution.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman has a third molar extracted on the left. Afterward the left anterior tongue feels numb to touch and temperature, and she also cannot taste sweet or salty solutions applied to that same region. Facial movement, tearing, and hearing are normal. Injury to which nerve best explains both deficits?

explanations.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries general sensation and taste from the posterior third of the tongue, which is not the affected area.
explanations.B: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to tongue musculature and its injury would cause deviation, not numbness.
explanations.C: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth and, through the mental nerve, the chin and lower lip.
explanations.D: The lingual nerve of V3 carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and is joined by the chorda tympani, which carries the taste fibers, so a single injury abolishes both modalities together.
explanations.E: The long buccal nerve supplies the mucosa and skin of the cheek rather than the tongue.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman has a benign tumor eroding the pterygopalatine fossa on the right. She reports that the roof of her throat behind the nose feels numb and that she no longer feels the passage of a nasal endoscope on that side, though the oropharynx feels normal. Taste and palatal elevation are unaffected. Which nerve provides the lost general sensation?

answers.A: Greater petrosal branch of the facial nerve
answers.B: Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve
answers.C: Lingual branch of the mandibular nerve
answers.D: Pharyngeal branch of the maxillary nerve
answers.E: Tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve

explanations.A: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers toward the pterygopalatine ganglion and taste from the palate.
explanations.B: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies general sensation to the laryngopharynx and the larynx above the vocal cords.
explanations.C: The lingual nerve supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth.
explanations.D: General sensation of the nasopharynx is carried by the pharyngeal nerve, a branch of the pterygopalatine nerves of the maxillary division, which traverses the pterygopalatine fossa.
explanations.E: The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the middle ear cavity and gives rise to the lesser petrosal nerve.

questions.question: A 57-year-old man receives a bilateral nerve block above the thyrohyoid membrane before an awake intubation. Afterward he cannot sense a catheter touching the mucosa above his vocal cords and does not cough when it contacts the epiglottis, although his vocal cords still move normally and his voice is unchanged. Which nerve was blocked?

answers.A: External laryngeal branch of the vagus
answers.C: Hypoglossal nerve to the tongue muscles
answers.D: Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus
answers.E: Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus

explanations.A: The external laryngeal nerve is motor to the cricothyroid muscle, so its block alters vocal pitch rather than sensation.
explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the oropharynx and the upper laryngopharynx but not the supraglottic larynx and epiglottis.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the muscles of the tongue and carries no sensory fibers.
explanations.D: The internal laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to supply general sensation above the vocal cords, forming the afferent limb of the cough reflex.
explanations.E: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles and the mucosa below the cords, and its block causes hoarseness.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman has a single small infarct in the tegmentum of the left rostral pons. She has decreased touch and vibration sensation over the right side of the face and over the right arm, trunk, and leg, all in one contiguous field, with normal strength. Her physician notes that one bundle completes the head portion of the sensory homunculus. Alongside which structure does the trigeminal lemniscus run?

explanations.A: The central tegmental tract is a motor integration pathway carrying rubro-olivary fibers.
explanations.B: The lateral lemniscus is a purely auditory bundle ascending to the inferior colliculus.
explanations.C: The trigeminal lemniscus travels at the medial edge of the medial lemniscus and functionally supplies the head portion that is otherwise missing from the ascending body representation, so a single lesion can numb the face and limbs together.
explanations.D: The medial longitudinal fasciculus coordinates eye and head movements and carries no somatosensory information.
explanations.E: The spinal trigeminal tract carries first-order pain fibers descending toward their nucleus and lies dorsolaterally.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has 2 years of progressive slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, emotional incontinence, and a spastic tongue without wasting. Tapping the chin produces an exaggerated, rapid jaw closure. Limb reflexes are also brisk with bilateral extensor plantar responses. This exaggerated jaw jerk indicates a lesion located where?

answers.A: Bilaterally above the mid-pons, in corticobulbar fibers
answers.B: In the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal bilaterally
answers.C: In the motor trigeminal nucleus bilaterally
answers.D: In the peripheral mandibular divisions bilaterally
answers.E: In the spinal trigeminal nucleus bilaterally

explanations.A: The jaw jerk is a monosynaptic stretch reflex whose arc lies entirely within the pons, so an exaggerated response indicates loss of descending corticobulbar inhibition from a bilateral upper motor neuron lesion above that level.
explanations.B: Loss of the mesencephalic nucleus would remove the afferent limb and abolish rather than exaggerate the reflex.
explanations.C: Destruction of the motor trigeminal nucleus removes the efferent limb and produces a flaccid, wasted jaw with an absent reflex.
explanations.D: Peripheral mandibular lesions interrupt both limbs of the arc and abolish the reflex.
explanations.E: The spinal trigeminal nucleus mediates facial pain and temperature and is not part of the jaw jerk circuit.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman has a small demyelinating plaque involving the dorsal cochlear nucleus on the left at the pontomedullary junction. Pure-tone thresholds are only mildly reduced on the left. Her physician traces the second-order axons that leave this nucleus and ascend in the lateral lemniscus. Where do those axons terminate?

explanations.A: Second-order fibers from the dorsal cochlear nucleus ascend directly in the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus, the major auditory integration center of the caudal midbrain.
explanations.B: The medial geniculate nucleus is reached only after a synapse in the inferior colliculus.
explanations.C: The superior colliculus receives retinal input and coordinates orienting movements of the head and eyes.
explanations.D: The superior olivary complex is the target of the ventral, not dorsal, cochlear nucleus.
explanations.E: The ventral posteromedial nucleus is a somatosensory relay for the head.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man has an infarct in the central tegmentum of the mid-pons. Audiometric thresholds are normal in both ears, but he can no longer tell which side a sound is coming from. His physician explains that fibers from one cochlear nucleus must reach the opposite side to allow comparison of arrival times. Which structure carries these decussating fibers?

explanations.A: The anterior white commissure carries crossing spinothalamic fibers within the spinal cord.
explanations.B: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries olivocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar fibers into the cerebellum.
explanations.C: Internal arcuate fibers are the decussating axons of the dorsal column nuclei in the caudal medulla.
explanations.D: The lateral lemniscus is the ascending bundle to the inferior colliculus and is not itself the site of decussation.
explanations.E: Ventral cochlear nucleus axons cross the mid-pons in the trapezoid body to reach the contralateral superior olivary complex, which computes interaural time differences for sound localization in the horizontal plane.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man has an infarct of the left temporal lobe. He hears sounds in both ears but cannot recognize speech or identify familiar melodies. Pure-tone thresholds are near normal bilaterally. His physician reviews the final relay that projects to the primary auditory cortex on the superior temporal gyrus. Which structure gives rise to that projection?

explanations.A: The cochlear nuclei are the first central relay and lie at the pontomedullary junction.
explanations.B: The inferior colliculus is an integration center that projects onward to the thalamus rather than to cortex directly.
explanations.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the thalamic relay for vision.
explanations.D: The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus receives fibers from the inferior colliculus and projects to the primary auditory cortex of the superior temporal gyrus for conscious perception.
explanations.E: The superior olivary complex contributes ascending fibers to the lateral lemniscus for sound localization.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman has progressive hearing loss confined to the right ear, with tinnitus and difficulty using the telephone on that side. Audiometry results are shown. Speech discrimination is disproportionately poor on the right. Which site of injury best explains a complete unilateral sensorineural hearing loss?

explanations.A: Auditory information becomes bilaterally represented immediately above the cochlear nuclei, so only a lesion at or peripheral to the cochlear nucleus can abolish hearing in one ear alone.
explanations.B: The inferior colliculus receives input from both ears, so a unilateral lesion does not cause unilateral deafness.
explanations.C: The lateral lemniscus already carries bilateral information after the trapezoid body decussation.
explanations.D: A medial geniculate lesion would degrade conscious perception bilaterally rather than produce a one-sided threshold shift.
explanations.E: The superior olivary complex receives input from both ventral cochlear nuclei, and its loss impairs localization with preserved thresholds.

questions.question: A 39-year-old man is being evaluated for a brainstem mass. On the histologic section his neurologist points out a pair of curved white matter bundles that resemble lobster claws grasping a large dorsal auditory nucleus, along with a small ovoid motor nucleus embedded in the medial longitudinal fasciculus. Which level does this section represent?

explanations.A: The caudal medulla shows the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus with the pyramidal and sensory decussations.
explanations.B: At the caudal midbrain the lateral lemnisci appear as lobster claws clasping the inferior colliculus, and the trochlear nucleus sits as an egg in the cup of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
explanations.C: The caudal pons shows the abducens and facial nuclei with the facial colliculus.
explanations.D: The mid-pons shows the motor and main sensory trigeminal nuclei, the trapezoid body, and the superior olivary complex.
explanations.E: The rostral midbrain shows the superior colliculus, red nucleus, substantia nigra, and oculomotor complex.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man has a slowly enlarging mass centered on the left dorsal cochlear nucleus. Over several weeks he develops headache worse in the morning, vomiting, and papilledema in addition to reduced hearing on the left. Imaging shows the mass now occludes the left lateral aperture of the fourth ventricle. Which complication best explains the new symptoms?

answers.A: Compression of the optic chiasm by the mass
answers.B: Direct invasion of the primary auditory cortex of the temporal lobe
answers.C: Impaired cerebrospinal fluid outflow with ventricular enlargement
answers.D: Interruption of the trigeminal lemniscus in the pons
answers.E: Occlusion of the internal auditory artery

explanations.A: The optic chiasm lies far rostrally beneath the hypothalamus and is not reachable from the pontomedullary junction.
explanations.B: The auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe and is not contiguous with this mass.
explanations.C: The lateral aperture, or foramen of Luschka, is an outflow route for cerebrospinal fluid from the fourth ventricle, and blocking it raises ventricular pressure, which also threatens nearby floor structures such as the vestibular, hypoglossal, and vagal nuclei.
explanations.D: Trigeminal lemniscus injury would cause contralateral facial numbness, not headache and papilledema.
explanations.E: Internal auditory artery occlusion causes sudden deafness and vertigo without raised intracranial pressure.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man has an infarct involving one of the vestibular nuclei. He is unsteady, falls toward the affected side, and has poor tone in the paravertebral and proximal extensor muscles when standing, but his extraocular movements are normal and he has no diplopia. Which vestibular nucleus is most likely involved?

explanations.A: The inferior vestibular nucleus is the most caudal nucleus and influences blood flow, respiratory rate, and heart rate on standing.
explanations.B: The lateral vestibular nucleus gives rise to vestibulospinal projections that maintain posture and balance by regulating paravertebral and proximal limb extensor tone.
explanations.C: The medial vestibular nucleus is the largest and mediates the vestibulo-ocular reflex and head and neck positioning.
explanations.D: The solitary nucleus is a visceral sensory nucleus for taste and baroreception and has no vestibular function.
explanations.E: The superior vestibular nucleus extends most rostrally and contributes to the vestibulo-ocular reflex and postural adjustment.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman has a right thalamic infarct. She reports a persistent sense that the room is tilted and that she cannot judge whether her head is upright, although she has no nystagmus, no hearing loss, and normal caloric-independent balance testing. Which thalamic nucleus receives the ascending vestibular projection that mediates conscious awareness of head position?

explanations.A: The anterior nucleus belongs to the limbic circuit connecting mammillary bodies to the cingulate gyrus.
explanations.B: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay.
explanations.C: The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay from the inferior colliculus.
explanations.D: The ventral posterolateral nucleus relays somatosensory input from the body.
explanations.E: Vestibular nuclei send ascending fibers to the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus, providing conscious awareness of head orientation and motion.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman has an infarct in the mid-medulla involving a vestibular nucleus that has a characteristically stippled appearance on histologic sections because of the many longitudinal axon bundles running through it. She becomes lightheaded with marked blood pressure and heart rate swings on standing. Which nucleus is involved?

explanations.A: The dorsal cochlear nucleus is auditory and lies at the pontomedullary junction wrapped over the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
explanations.B: The inferior or descending vestibular nucleus is the most caudal, extends into the mid-medulla, has a stippled appearance from its longitudinal fiber bundles, and influences blood flow, heart rate, and respiration with changes in posture.
explanations.C: The lateral vestibular nucleus is confined to the caudal pons and drives vestibulospinal postural reflexes.
explanations.D: The medial vestibular nucleus appears more uniformly pale and mediates the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
