explanations.E: The superior vestibular nucleus is the most rostral, extending up to the mid-pons.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is comatose after a drug overdose. When his head is briskly rotated to the right, both eyes deviate conjugately to the left and then slowly return to midline, indicating an intact brainstem. Corneal reflexes and pupillary responses are also preserved. The afferent limb of the reflex being tested arises from which structure?

answers.B: Neck muscle spindles and the mesencephalic nucleus
answers.D: Semicircular canals and the vestibular nerve
answers.E: Superior colliculus and the superior brachium

explanations.A: The cochlea and spiral ganglion transduce sound and project to the cochlear nuclei, not to the extraocular motor nuclei.
explanations.B: Neck proprioception contributes to postural control, and the mesencephalic nucleus serves the muscles of mastication only.
explanations.C: Retinal input is not required, which is why the reflex persists with the eyes covered and in comatose patients.
explanations.D: Angular acceleration detected by the semicircular canals is carried by the vestibular division of CN VIII to the vestibular nuclei, which then drive the extraocular motor nuclei through the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
explanations.E: The superior colliculus mediates voluntary orienting and saccadic behavior rather than the oculocephalic reflex.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has a small medullary lesion after a vertebral artery dissection. Testing results are shown. She has no facial weakness, normal tearing, and normal salivary flow, and general sensation over the tongue is intact throughout. Which structure is most likely damaged?

answers.C: Right main sensory nucleus of the trigeminal

explanations.A: The chorda tympani carries taste only from the anterior two-thirds, so its injury would spare the posterior third.
explanations.B: A lingual nerve lesion would abolish general sensation of the anterior tongue as well, and touch is preserved.
explanations.C: The main sensory nucleus handles light touch and pressure rather than taste.
explanations.D: Taste fibers from cranial nerves VII, IX, and X all converge on the solitary nucleus and tract, so a single medullary lesion abolishes taste over the entire hemitongue while leaving general sensation intact.
explanations.E: The spinal trigeminal nucleus mediates pain and temperature from the head, not taste.

questions.question: A 51-year-old man has a tumor at the jugular foramen. He can taste sugar placed on the tip and sides of his tongue but cannot taste quinine placed on the back of the tongue on the right, and the right oropharynx is numb. Tearing, facial movement, and voice are normal. Which nerve carries the taste fibers that are lost?

answers.A: Chorda tympani of the facial nerve
answers.D: Lingual nerve of the mandibular division

explanations.A: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds, which is preserved.
explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries both taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue and the oropharynx, so its injury produces exactly this combination.
explanations.C: The greater petrosal nerve carries palatal taste and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the lacrimal gland.
explanations.D: The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the anterior tongue rather than taste from the posterior third.
explanations.E: The vagus nerve carries only a small amount of taste from the epiglottis, and his voice is normal.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has an infarct involving a single nucleus in the rostral medulla. He has complete ipsilateral loss of taste from the anterior tongue, the posterior tongue, and the epiglottis, with preserved general sensation everywhere and normal palatal movement. Which set of cranial nerves converges on the damaged structure to produce this pattern?

answers.A: Cranial nerves III, IV, and VI
answers.B: Cranial nerves IX, X, and XII
answers.C: Cranial nerves V, IX, and X
answers.D: Cranial nerves V, VII, and IX
answers.E: Cranial nerves VII, IX, and X

explanations.A: These are the somatic motor nerves to the extraocular muscles and carry no sensory information.
explanations.B: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue and carries no taste.
explanations.C: Although IX and X contribute taste, the trigeminal nerve does not, and the facial contribution to the anterior tongue would be unexplained.
explanations.D: The trigeminal nerve carries general sensation from the tongue but no taste fibers to the solitary nucleus.
explanations.E: The solitary nucleus is the single visceral sensory nucleus receiving taste from CN VII by the chorda tympani, from CN IX for the posterior third, and from CN X for the epiglottis.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman undergoes an aortic arch procedure and afterward has wide swings in heart rate and blood pressure with position changes. Findings are shown. Carotid sinus massage still slows her heart rate normally, indicating that the glossopharyngeal afferent limb is intact. Which nerve carries the baroreceptor afferents from the aortic arch?

explanations.A: The facial nerve carries taste and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers but no baroreceptor input.
explanations.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input from the carotid sinus and body, which is explicitly preserved here.
explanations.C: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue.
explanations.D: The trigeminal nerve carries general somatic sensation from the head and no visceral afferents from great vessels.
explanations.E: The vagus nerve carries baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents from the aortic arch and aortic bodies to the caudal portion of the solitary nucleus.

questions.question: A 57-year-old man has a small infarct restricted to the rostral portion of the right solitary nucleus. Taste is absent over the right side of the tongue. His blood pressure and heart rate responses to standing, to carotid sinus massage, and to Valsalva are entirely normal. Which functional property best explains the preserved cardiovascular responses?

answers.A: Baroreceptor afferents bypass the solitary nucleus entirely
answers.B: Baroreceptor afferents terminate in the caudal portion of the nucleus
answers.C: Baroreceptor afferents terminate in the nucleus ambiguus directly
answers.D: Taste and baroreceptor fibers both project to the spinal trigeminal nucleus
answers.E: Taste fibers decussate before reaching the solitary nucleus

explanations.A: Baroreceptor afferents from CN IX and CN X definitely terminate in the solitary nucleus and do not bypass it.
explanations.B: The solitary nucleus is functionally segregated, with taste input arriving rostrally and baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input arriving caudally, so a rostral lesion abolishes taste while sparing cardiovascular reflexes.
explanations.C: The nucleus ambiguus provides the efferent cardiac limb rather than receiving primary visceral afferents.
explanations.D: The spinal trigeminal nucleus handles pain and temperature from the head and receives neither taste nor baroreceptor fibers.
explanations.E: Taste fibers reach the solitary nucleus ipsilaterally, which is why the deficit is one-sided.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has a biopsy of the circumvallate papillae, a row of large papillae situated just in front of the sulcus terminalis on the dorsum of the tongue. Afterward she notes reduced taste from this region, though taste at the tip of the tongue and general sensation of the anterior tongue are normal. Which nerve supplies taste to these papillae?

explanations.A: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but does not reach the circumvallate papillae.
explanations.B: Despite lying just anterior to the sulcus terminalis, the circumvallate papillae take their taste innervation from the glossopharyngeal nerve, which serves the posterior third of the tongue.
explanations.C: The greater petrosal nerve carries taste from the palate.
explanations.D: The lingual nerve carries general sensation, not taste, from the anterior tongue.
explanations.E: The vagus nerve carries taste only from the epiglottis and adjacent laryngopharynx.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man has an infarct that destroys the right lateral lemniscus in the mid-pons. He has mild difficulty localizing sounds and following conversation in noisy rooms, but audiometry demonstrates only minimally elevated thresholds and no unilateral deafness. Which feature of the auditory pathway best explains the preserved hearing in both ears?

answers.A: Auditory fibers become bilaterally represented at the trapezoid body
answers.B: Both cochleae project to a single midline auditory nucleus
answers.C: Each lateral lemniscus receives input only from the opposite cochlea
answers.D: The inferior colliculus projects bilaterally to both auditory cortices
answers.E: The medial geniculate nucleus receives direct input from both cochleae

explanations.A: Ventral cochlear nucleus fibers cross in the trapezoid body to reach both superior olivary complexes, so each lateral lemniscus carries information from both ears and a unilateral lesion above this point cannot deafen one ear.
explanations.B: There is no single midline auditory nucleus; the cochlear and olivary nuclei are paired.
explanations.C: Each lateral lemniscus carries a mixture of crossed and uncrossed fibers rather than input from one cochlea.
explanations.D: Bilateral cortical projection from a single colliculus is not the mechanism, and this would not explain preserved thresholds.
explanations.E: The medial geniculate nucleus receives fibers from the inferior colliculus, not directly from the cochlea.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman has a schwannoma arising from the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve. She has progressive right-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and unsteadiness, and later develops a diminished right corneal reflex. At which site does the affected nerve enter the brainstem?

answers.B: Lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction
answers.C: Middle cerebellar peduncle at the mid-pons

explanations.A: The interpeduncular fossa is the exit point of the oculomotor nerve from the midbrain.
explanations.B: The vestibulocochlear nerve enters at the lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction, close to the facial nerve at the cerebellopontine angle, which explains why a growing mass here later compresses the trigeminal root.
explanations.C: The middle cerebellar peduncle transmits the trigeminal roots at the mid-pons.
explanations.D: The post-olivary sulcus transmits the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
explanations.E: The pre-olivary sulcus transmits the hypoglossal nerve rootlets.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man undergoes resection of a suprasellar craniopharyngioma. Postoperatively his visual fields and acuity are stable, but his sleep and wake times drift progressively later each day and no longer track the light-dark cycle. Retinal fibers mediating this entrainment project to which structure?

answers.C: Lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus

explanations.A: A subset of retinal ganglion cell axons leaves the primary visual pathway to reach the hypothalamus, where supraoptic and adjacent nuclei entrain circadian rhythms to the light-dark cycle.
explanations.B: The inferior colliculus is an auditory relay with no retinal input.
explanations.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays conscious vision to the occipital cortex, and acuity and fields are preserved here.
explanations.D: The pretectal nuclei mediate the pupillary light reflex by projecting to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
explanations.E: The superior colliculus coordinates orienting movements of the head and eyes rather than circadian timing.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman has a lesion of the dorsal rostral midbrain. Visual acuity, fields, and pupillary reactions are normal, but she no longer turns her head and eyes automatically toward an object appearing suddenly in the periphery, and her smooth pursuit and fixation are impaired. First-order retinal fibers reach the affected structure by which route?

answers.A: Inferior brachium to the inferior colliculus
answers.B: Lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus
answers.C: Optic radiations from the lateral geniculate nucleus
answers.D: Superior brachium to the superior colliculus
answers.E: Trigeminal lemniscus to the ventral posteromedial nucleus

explanations.A: The inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus and carries auditory information.
explanations.B: The lateral lemniscus is the ascending auditory pathway to the inferior colliculus.
explanations.C: The optic radiations carry third-order fibers to the primary visual cortex and are not involved in reflex orienting.
explanations.D: First-order retinal axons travel in the superior brachium directly to the superior colliculus, bypassing the thalamic relay, and this structure coordinates orienting movements of the head and eyes as well as fixation, smooth pursuit, saccades, and vergence.
explanations.E: The trigeminal lemniscus carries somatosensory information from the head to the thalamus.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman has blurred vision when reading and diplopia on lateral gaze. On leftward gaze the right eye fails to adduct while the left eye abducts with nystagmus, yet when she fixates on a pen brought toward her nose both eyes converge normally and both pupils constrict. Which explanation best accounts for the preserved convergence?

answers.A: Convergence is driven by a midbrain pathway that bypasses the medial longitudinal fasciculus
answers.B: Convergence is mediated by the abducens nucleus rather than the oculomotor nucleus
answers.C: Convergence uses the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus instead of the ipsilateral one
answers.D: The medial rectus receives innervation from the trochlear nucleus during near effort
answers.E: The paramedian pontine reticular formation drives both medial recti during near effort

explanations.A: The oculomotor nucleus can be activated directly for convergence without receiving an internuclear signal through the medial longitudinal fasciculus, so the medial rectus still works during near effort even when the tract is destroyed.
explanations.B: The abducens nucleus drives abduction and the internuclear pathway for conjugate gaze, not convergence.
explanations.C: Convergence does not require either medial longitudinal fasciculus, and a contralateral route would still be an internuclear pathway.
explanations.D: The trochlear nucleus supplies only the superior oblique muscle.
explanations.E: The paramedian pontine reticular formation generates conjugate horizontal saccades rather than disconjugate vergence movements.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with hypertension has sudden diplopia. Neither eye moves to the left of the midline on command or on pursuit, while both eyes move fully to the right and the right eye adducts normally during right gaze. Convergence, vertical gaze, pupils, and facial strength are all normal. Which structure is most likely infarcted?

explanations.A: An abducens nerve lesion would prevent only left eye abduction while the right eye would still adduct fully on left gaze.
explanations.B: The abducens nucleus contains both the motor neurons for the left lateral rectus and the internuclear neurons that cross and ascend to the right oculomotor nucleus, so its destruction abolishes all conjugate gaze toward the left.
explanations.C: A left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion would impair left eye adduction on right gaze, but right gaze is normal.
explanations.D: A right medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion would impair right eye adduction on left gaze while leaving left eye abduction intact.
explanations.E: A right paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion would abolish conjugate gaze to the right rather than to the left.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is undergoing functional imaging while performing rapid voluntary eye movements from one target to another. Activation is seen in the lateral frontal lobe just rostral to the portion of the primary motor cortex devoted to eye movement. To generate a horizontal saccade, this region projects most directly to which structure?

answers.B: Ipsilateral abducens nucleus in the caudal pons
answers.C: Ipsilateral superior colliculus of the midbrain
answers.D: Ipsilateral trochlear nucleus in the caudal midbrain
answers.E: Ipsilateral vestibular nuclei of the pontomedullary junction

explanations.A: The frontal eye field projects to the paramedian pontine reticular formation of the opposite side, which then drives the adjacent abducens nucleus and, through the medial longitudinal fasciculus, the contralateral oculomotor nucleus to produce a conjugate saccade.
explanations.B: The abducens nucleus is reached by way of the paramedian pontine reticular formation rather than directly from cortex.
explanations.C: The superior colliculus participates in reflexive orienting and receives retinal input but is not the direct saccadic relay described here.
explanations.D: The trochlear nucleus governs the superior oblique and vertical movements.
explanations.E: The vestibular nuclei drive compensatory eye movements during head motion, not voluntary saccades.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg, left facial droop sparing the forehead, and neglect of the left side of space. Her eyes rest deviated toward the right and she cannot look to the left on command, but the eyes cross the midline fully when her head is passively rotated. Which site is most likely infarcted?

explanations.A: A left-sided cortical lesion would deviate the eyes toward the left and cause right-sided weakness.
explanations.B: A left pontine gaze center lesion would abolish leftward gaze even with the oculocephalic maneuver.
explanations.C: A destructive frontal eye field lesion removes the drive for contralateral gaze, so the eyes deviate toward the lesion and away from the hemiparesis, and because the brainstem circuitry is intact the deviation can be overcome by the oculocephalic reflex.
explanations.D: A right pontine gaze center lesion would deviate the eyes to the left, toward the weak side, and could not be overcome by head rotation.
explanations.E: A superior colliculus lesion impairs reflexive orienting rather than producing a fixed conjugate deviation with hemineglect.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man has a lesion that interrupts the fibers leaving the dentate nucleus of the left cerebellum. He has clumsiness and intention tremor of the left arm. His physician traces this limb of the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit as it crosses the midline to reach the red nucleus of the opposite side. Which structure carries these axons out of the cerebellum?

explanations.A: The central tegmental tract carries the rubro-olivary limb from the red nucleus down to the inferior olive.
explanations.B: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries olivocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar fibers into the cerebellum.
explanations.C: The lateral lemniscus is a purely auditory bundle ascending to the inferior colliculus.
explanations.D: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibers from the basal pontine nuclei into the contralateral cerebellum.
explanations.E: Dentate output, including the dentatorubral tract, leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and decussates in the midbrain to reach the contralateral red nucleus.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman has an infarct of the right inferior olivary complex in the rostral medulla. Her physician explains that olivary neurons normally send axons through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the opposite cerebellar cortex, where they exert a powerful excitatory influence on Purkinje cells. What are these axons called once they reach the cerebellum?

explanations.A: Basket cells are inhibitory interneurons intrinsic to the cerebellar cortex.
explanations.B: Olivocerebellar axons become climbing fibers, which wrap around Purkinje cell dendrites and provide strong excitatory input used in motor learning.
explanations.C: Mossy fibers arise from pontine, spinal, and vestibular sources and synapse on granule cells rather than directly on Purkinje cells.
explanations.D: Parallel fibers are the axons of granule cells running through the molecular layer.
explanations.E: Purkinje cell axons are the inhibitory output of the cerebellar cortex to the deep nuclei.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is found at autopsy to have selective loss of neurons in the ventral portion of the substantia nigra, dorsal to the cerebral peduncles, with the more dorsal pigmented band relatively preserved. During life he had abnormal involuntary movements rather than rigidity. Loss of which cell population accounts for the affected ventral band?

answers.A: Dopaminergic neurons of the pars compacta projecting to the striatum
answers.B: GABAergic neurons of the pars reticulata projecting to the thalamus
answers.C: Glutamatergic neurons of the subthalamic nucleus projecting to the pallidum
answers.D: Noradrenergic neurons of the locus ceruleus projecting to the cortex
answers.E: Serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei projecting to the dorsal horn

explanations.A: The dopaminergic pars compacta lies dorsally, contains the neuromelanin that blackens the nucleus, and its loss causes the rigidity and bradykinesia of Parkinson disease.
explanations.B: The pars reticulata occupies the ventral portion of the substantia nigra and contains GABAergic neurons that tonically inhibit the thalamus as an output station of the basal nuclei.
explanations.C: The subthalamic nucleus is a diencephalic structure and is not part of the substantia nigra.
explanations.D: The locus ceruleus lies in the dorsal rostral pons beside the fourth ventricle.
explanations.E: The raphe nuclei lie along the midline seam of the brainstem tegmentum and modulate pain and mood.

questions.question: At autopsy of a 79-year-old man, the pathologist sections the brainstem and notes a small paired structure in the dorsal tegmentum of the rostral pons, just lateral to the fourth ventricle, that appears sapphire blue to nearly black because of accumulated neuromelanin. During life the patient had marked daytime hypervigilance and an exaggerated startle. Which structure is described?

explanations.A: The inferior olivary complex lies in the rostral medulla and appears as a crenated ribbon of grey matter without pigment.
explanations.B: The locus ceruleus is the small pigmented nucleus in the dorsal rostral pons lateral to the fourth ventricle, and its noradrenergic neurons drive vigilance, attention, and startle responses.
explanations.C: The raphe nuclei lie along the midline throughout the tegmentum and are not visibly pigmented.
explanations.D: The red nucleus sits in the rostral midbrain and owes its pink hue to vascularity rather than neuromelanin.
explanations.E: The substantia nigra is also pigmented but lies in the rostral midbrain immediately dorsal to the cerebral peduncles.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman is treated with a drug that reduces the activity of a small pigmented brainstem nucleus that is normally silent during sleep and maximally active during startle and heightened watchfulness. She becomes calmer and less easily startled, and her resting tremor is unchanged. Which neurotransmitter is released by the neurons of this nucleus?

explanations.A: Acetylcholine is used by cholinergic pontine and basal forebrain systems that promote REM sleep and cortical activation.
explanations.B: Dopamine is supplied to the striatum by the substantia nigra pars compacta.
explanations.C: Gamma-aminobutyric acid is the transmitter of pars reticulata output neurons and local inhibitory interneurons.
explanations.D: The locus ceruleus is the principal source of norepinephrine in the central nervous system and projects widely to cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, cerebellum, and spinal cord to heighten arousal and vigilance.
explanations.E: Serotonin is supplied by the raphe nuclei, whose activity declines gradually through non-REM sleep rather than ceasing abruptly.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a small midline brainstem lesion develops both a persistently depressed mood and a marked increase in the intensity of chronic low back pain that had previously been tolerable. Imaging shows a lesion along the midline seam of the tegmentum. Which structure is most likely involved?

explanations.A: The locus ceruleus is the noradrenergic source for arousal and vigilance and lies laterally in the dorsal rostral pons.
explanations.B: The periaqueductal gray surrounds the cerebral aqueduct and relays to the raphe nuclei but is not a midline tegmental seam structure with widespread cortical projections.
explanations.C: The raphe nuclei sit along the midline throughout the tegmentum and are the principal serotonergic source, sending descending fibers that inhibit nociception in the dorsal horn and ascending fibers to limbic and cortical regions that influence mood.
explanations.D: The red nucleus participates in the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit for motor learning.
explanations.E: The substantia nigra pars compacta supplies dopamine to the striatum for movement control.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman with metastatic cancer obtains excellent relief of diffuse pain with an opioid. Her physician explains that ascending nociceptive fibers give off collateral branches to a rim of grey matter surrounding the cerebral aqueduct, which then recruits a descending inhibitory serotonergic system. Which structure receives these spinothalamic collaterals?

explanations.A: The inferior olivary complex participates in the motor learning loop with the red nucleus and cerebellum.
explanations.B: The locus ceruleus modulates arousal and attention through noradrenergic projections.
explanations.C: The periaqueductal gray surrounds the cerebral aqueduct, receives spinothalamic collaterals, and projects to the raphe nuclei, whose descending serotonergic fibers inhibit nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn; opioids act at all three levels.
explanations.D: The red nucleus is a motor integration station and not part of the analgesic circuit.
explanations.E: The pars reticulata inhibits the thalamus as an output nucleus of the basal nuclei.

questions.question: A 59-year-old man has increased extensor tone and impaired postural adjustment after a brainstem lesion. His physician reviews the two descending reticulospinal systems and notes that one arises rostrally and projects only to the same side of the spinal cord, while the other arises more caudally and projects bilaterally. Which structure gives rise to the ipsilateral, medial reticulospinal tract?

explanations.A: The lateral vestibular nucleus gives rise to the vestibulospinal tract rather than a reticulospinal tract.
explanations.B: The medullary reticular formation gives rise to the lateral reticulospinal tract, which projects bilaterally.
explanations.C: The pontine reticular formation gives rise to the medial reticulospinal tract, which projects ipsilaterally and, as part of the extrapyramidal system, facilitates locomotion, posture, and spinal reflexes.
explanations.D: The red nucleus gives rise to the rubrospinal tract and to rubro-olivary fibers in the central tegmental tract.
explanations.E: The superior colliculus gives rise to tectospinal fibers used in orienting the head toward stimuli.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is unresponsive after a hemorrhage in the paramedian tegmentum extending from the rostral pons into the midbrain bilaterally. His findings are shown. Pupillary, corneal, and gag reflexes are preserved and he breathes spontaneously, but he cannot be roused by any stimulus. Damage to which structure best explains his state?

answers.B: Corticospinal tracts in the medullary pyramids

explanations.A: The ascending reticular activating system within the paramedian tegmentum modulates wakefulness and responsiveness to sensory input, and bilateral damage produces coma with otherwise intact brainstem reflexes.
explanations.B: Bilateral pyramidal injury would produce quadriparesis in an awake patient rather than unresponsiveness.
explanations.C: Bilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus injury causes disordered conjugate gaze without altering consciousness.
explanations.D: Loss of the medullary raphe nuclei alters pain modulation and mood rather than producing coma.
explanations.E: Bilateral vestibular nuclear injury causes severe vertigo, nystagmus, and imbalance in a fully alert patient.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman has a hemorrhage involving the tegmentum of the medulla. She has an irregular breathing pattern with variable depth and irregular pauses, requiring intubation, and her blood pressure fluctuates widely without an obvious cause. Arterial blood gas results before intubation are shown. Which structure is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanations.A: The ascending reticular activating system governs arousal and consciousness rather than respiratory rhythm.
explanations.B: The reticular formation of the medulla contains the centers that set respiratory rhythm and depth and that regulate heart rate and blood pressure, so damage there produces ataxic breathing with labile hemodynamics.
explanations.C: The nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles and cardiac parasympathetics but does not generate respiratory rhythm.
explanations.D: The solitary nucleus receives visceral afferents and feeds this information into the reticular formation rather than generating the pattern itself.
explanations.E: The vestibular nuclei influence circulatory adjustments with posture but do not set breathing patterns.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man has sudden weakness of the right arm and leg with decreased vibration and position sense on the right, while pain and temperature sensation are entirely normal throughout. His tongue deviates to the left on protrusion, and facial sensation, hearing, and palatal elevation are normal. Occlusion of which artery best explains these findings?

explanations.A: This vessel supplies the lateral pons, producing ipsilateral deafness, facial paralysis, and crossed sensory loss.
explanations.B: Branches of the anterior spinal artery supply the medial medulla, where the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus lie side by side, producing contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of vibration and position sense, and ipsilateral tongue deviation.
explanations.C: Basilar occlusion produces bilateral long tract signs and often a locked-in state.
explanations.D: This vessel supplies the lateral medulla, producing hoarseness, dysphagia, crossed pain and temperature loss, ataxia, and Horner syndrome.
explanations.E: This vessel supplies the rostral cerebellum and upper pons, causing prominent limb and gait ataxia.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man has sudden vertigo, vomiting, and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, with left limb dysmetria. His physician must decide whether the lesion is in the lateral medulla or the lateral pons. Which additional finding would best indicate that the lateral pons rather than the lateral medulla is involved?

answers.A: Contralateral loss of vibration sense in the arm and leg
answers.B: Ipsilateral hearing loss with complete facial paralysis
answers.D: Loss of the gag reflex with a hoarse, breathy voice
answers.E: Vertical gaze palsy with an unreactive dilated pupil

explanations.A: Loss of vibration sense implicates the medial lemniscus in a medial rather than lateral territory.
explanations.B: The cochlear nuclei and the facial nucleus lie in the lateral caudal pons, so deafness and a complete peripheral facial palsy indicate a lateral pontine lesion, typically from anterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion.
explanations.C: Tongue deviation reflects hypoglossal involvement in the medial medulla.
explanations.D: Hoarseness and an absent gag reflect nucleus ambiguus injury, which is characteristic of the lateral medulla.
explanations.E: Vertical gaze and pupillary findings localize to the midbrain, well above either candidate site.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman has a sudden left hemiparesis with a left central facial droop. The right eye is deviated down and out with complete ptosis and a fixed dilated right pupil. Sensation is normal throughout and there is no ataxia or tremor. Which site of injury best explains these findings?

answers.A: Dorsal midbrain at the superior colliculus
answers.E: Ventral midbrain at the cerebral peduncle

explanations.A: A dorsal midbrain lesion produces impaired upgaze and pupillary light-near dissociation without hemiparesis.
explanations.B: A lateral medullary lesion causes crossed sensory loss, hoarseness, ataxia, and Horner syndrome.
explanations.C: A lateral pontine lesion adds deafness and peripheral facial paralysis rather than a third nerve palsy.
explanations.D: A medial medullary lesion causes tongue deviation with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of vibration sense.
explanations.E: Oculomotor fibers pass through the ventral midbrain to exit at the interpeduncular fossa directly adjacent to the descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers of the cerebral peduncle, so a single lesion yields an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a basilar artery thrombosis is quadriplegic and unable to speak, swallow, or move his face, and horizontal gaze is absent in both directions. He is fully awake, follows all commands using vertical eye movements and blinking, and sensation appears intact. His findings are shown. Where is the lesion?

explanations.A: Bilateral thalamic infarction impairs arousal and produces a depressed level of consciousness rather than full wakefulness.
explanations.B: Bilateral destruction of the ventral pons interrupts the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts and the abducens nuclei while sparing the dorsal tegmental reticular activating system and the midbrain vertical gaze centers, producing the locked-in state.
explanations.C: A dorsal midbrain lesion impairs vertical gaze, which is preserved and is the patient's means of communication.
explanations.D: A lateral medullary lesion produces crossed sensory findings and bulbar signs without quadriplegia.
explanations.E: Isolated pyramidal lesions cause quadriparesis without loss of horizontal gaze or facial movement.

questions.question: A 59-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg. His entire right face is paralyzed including the forehead, and the right eye cannot abduct, though vertical gaze and pupillary responses are normal. Facial sensation is intact and he is fully alert. Which site of injury best accounts for this combination of findings?

explanations.A: A left-sided pontine lesion would paralyze the left face and weaken the right limbs.
explanations.B: A capsular lesion produces contralateral weakness with forehead sparing and no abduction deficit.
explanations.C: Crossed findings, meaning ipsilateral cranial nerve signs with contralateral long tract signs, localize the lesion to the brainstem, and the combination of a complete peripheral facial palsy with a lateral rectus palsy places it in the caudal pons where the facial and abducens nuclei lie together.
explanations.D: A right capsular lesion would weaken the left limbs but spare the forehead and eye movements.
explanations.E: A rostral midbrain lesion would produce a third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil rather than facial and abducens findings.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman with a lateral medullary infarct has hoarseness, dysphagia, crossed pain and temperature loss, and left limb ataxia. She also has a mildly drooping left upper lid, a small left pupil that reacts normally to light, and decreased sweating on the left side of her face. Interruption of which structure best explains this triad?

answers.B: Inferior cerebellar peduncle and juxtarestiform body
answers.C: Nucleus ambiguus of the rostral medulla
answers.D: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and its descending tract
answers.E: Spinothalamic tract of the anterolateral system

explanations.A: Sympathetic fibers descend uncrossed from the hypothalamus through the lateral brainstem tegmentum toward the upper thoracic cord, so their interruption produces an ipsilateral Horner syndrome with partial ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.
explanations.B: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries vestibular and olivary fibers into the cerebellum and its loss explains the ipsilateral limb ataxia.
explanations.C: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the palate, pharynx, and larynx and accounts for the hoarseness and dysphagia.
explanations.D: The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract account for the ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation.
explanations.E: The spinothalamic tract carries already-crossed fibers and accounts for the contralateral body pain and temperature loss.
